This website provides free tools (see table below) for calculating Biological
Condition Gradient (BCG) level assignments, BCG input and flag metrics,
temperature-related outputs and a biodiversity index for macroinvertebrate
assemblages in freshwater wadeable streams in Oregon and Washington. At the 
bottom of this page, we included a brief primer on the BCG along with links to
more detailed resources.

For those who prefer to use R instead of this online calculator, the BCG and
thermal preference calculations are carried out by the 
<a href="https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=BCGcalc" target="_blank">BCGcalc</a>
 and 
<a href="https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=BioMonTools" target="_blank">BioMonTools</a>
R packages, which are available on GitHub and were developed by Erik W. Leppo 
from Tetra Tech (Erik.Leppo@tetratech.com). If using the R code instead of the
Shiny app, you won’t need internet access if you have R installed on your 
computer and have downloaded all the necessary packages.

```{r}
# data
dn_shiny <- file.path("apps", "BCGcalc", "external", "RMD")
df_table <- readxl::read_xlsx(
  file.path("files",
            "About_CalculationTypes_20261030_mod.xlsx"))
# display
knitr::kable(df_table)
```

## What is the Biological Condition Gradient
![Figure 2. The Biological Condition Gradient (BCG), modified from Davies and Jackson 2006. The BCG was developed to serve as a scientific framework to synthesize expert knowledge with empirical observations and develop testable hypotheses on the response of aquatic biota to increasing levels of stress.](images/About_Fig2_BCG.jpg)

The Biological Condition Gradient (BCG) model is a conceptual model describing 
how ecological attributes change in response to increasing levels of 
human-caused stress. The BCG has a universal scoring scale with six levels of
biological condition, ranging from observable biological conditions found at no
or low levels of stressors (level 1) to those found at high levels of stressors
(level 6). Narratives for each BCG level are shown in the figure above. The 
model is calibrated using expert elicitation. Biologists work collaboratively 
to reach consensus on assigning biological samples to BCG levels. Their ratings
and rationale are then used to calibrate a quantitative model. Model performance
is judged based on how well the model matches the expert BCG level assignments.
